reason: There are 16 claims supported by at least two independent sites, providing a wealth of detail about the planet's composition, origins, and extreme environment.
story: In 2011, astronomers discovered a cosmic treasure 4,000 light-years away: a planet made of diamond. This isn’t just a shiny rock; it’s the crystallized corpse of a dead star. Originally a Sun-like star in a binary pair, its neighbor exploded into a pulsar. Over billions of years, the pulsar’s intense gravity siphoned away 99.9% of the star’s mass, stripping it down to its white dwarf core. The remaining carbon and oxygen are so compressed they formed a crystal structure denser than platinum. This "Diamond Planet," known as PSR J1719-1438 b, orbits its host every 130 minutes. The entire system is so compact that the planet’s orbit would fit inside our own Sun. The pulsar itself is a tiny, city-sized sphere only 12 miles wide, yet it spins 10,000 times a minute. It’s a rare survivor of a stellar heist, transformed by extreme pressure into a massive, spacefaring gem.
angle: This planet is the diamond-crystallized core of a dead star that had 99.9% of its mass stolen by its pulsar neighbor.

claims.claim: PSR J1719−1438 b was discovered or published on August 25, 2011.
The planet orbits a millisecond pulsar named PSR J1719-1438.
The system is located approximately 4,000 light-years from Earth.
The pulsar host star rotates more than 10,000 times per minute.
The pulsar has a mass approximately 1.4 times that of the Sun.
The pulsar is only about 12 miles or 20 kilometers in diameter.
The planet orbits its host in approximately 2 hours and 10 minutes.
The planet is composed primarily of carbon and oxygen.
The planet's density is at least 23 grams per cubic centimeter.
The planet is at least 20 times as dense as Jupiter, making it denser than platinum.
The planet is about 60,000 kilometers in diameter, making it five times the size of Earth.
The planet is the remnant of a star that lost more than 99.9% of its mass.
The entire orbital system would fit inside the diameter of the Sun.
The discovery was made using the 64-meter Parkes radio telescope in Australia.
The system is located in the constellation Serpens.
The planet has a mass similar to that of Jupiter.

disputed: One study from 2012 suggested the planet might actually be a 1-kilometer lump of quark matter rather than a white dwarf remnant; the script should focus on the primary diamond planet theory but note it as the leading explanation.

Whether the planet would actually sparkle like a diamond is speculative; the script should attribute the idea of it 'sparkling' to specific scientist quotes or frame it as a possibility under high-pressure crystallization.
